description:

Read each poem twice. For each poem:

  1. Paraphrase one difficult sentence or passage, following the syntax across the line breaks.

  2. Mark one consequential choice—repetition, pronouns, imagery, punctuation, or a line break—and explain its effect.

  3. Identify one uncertainty or question about the language.

name: Journal Check #1
description:
You will write by hand in your journal during most class periods. These entries are designed to help you warm up your thinking, prepare for discussion, reflect on ideas, do creative exercises, and draft work before it becomes polished or formal.

This journal is a low-stakes space for thinking and exploration, not for perfect writing. What matters is consistent engagement and effort.

This grade reflects your engagement and completion of journal entries from the beginning of the semester through the first journal review. Journals are assessed for consistency, effort, and engagement with prompts and ideas, not for polish or correctness.


What You're Being Assessed On

  • Writing consistently during class

  • Responding thoughtfully to prompts, texts, and discussions

  • Showing evidence of effort and engagement

  • Using the journal as a space to think, question, and explore ideas

You are not graded on grammar, spelling, or polish.

Occasional checkmarks or brief comments may appear, but detailed feedback is not provided.


Rubric

45-50 points Consistently Engaged Journal includes entries for nearly every class session, stays on task, and shows clear effort and thinking.
40-44 points Generally Engaged Journal includes most entries, shows effort, and is usually on task, though some entries may be surface-level.
30-39 points Inconsistently Engaged Journal is missing multiple entries or shows uneven effort and focus.
below 30 points Minimally Engaged Many entries are missing or off-task, with limited evidence of effort.

name: Unit 1 Harkness Discussion
description:
Class Discussion Norms

Harkness Discussion Guidelines

 

In this discussion, we will use Emily Dickinson's poems to reconsider the questions we have pursued throughout Unit 1: The American "I" and "We."

Prepare for the discussion

  • Read and annotate all eight Dickinson poems. Revisit the Unit 1 poems you might bring into conversation with them.

  • Bring two specific poems (with specific lines/quotes) you want to discuss. They may be two Dickinson poems or from Dickinson and another Unit 1 poet.

  • Come with at least one question you want to discuss with the class. Be ready to point to a specific word, image, pattern, or formal choice that relates to the question.

  • You may bring an idea you are considering for Friday's in-class assessment, but you do not need a finished claim.


During the discussion
Help the group build an interpretation. Read closely, explain how details shape meaning, listen and respond to others, and make connections that lead us somewhere new. You may challenge a claim, revise your own, or identify an uncertainty the group should investigate. A thoughtful contribution can be a question or a careful response; it need not be a speech.


This is a minor assignment worth 50 points. Scroll down to see the rubric.


Unit 1 Harkness Discussion sheet: https://docs.google.com/document/d/GOOGLE_DOC_ID_40/edit?usp=sharing

 

Rubric

Close Reading

Grounds ideas in specific poems, stanzas, lines, or quotes; explains how words, images, or formal choices create effects

 20
Development of Ideas

Advances an interpretation, tests it, complicates it, or draws a meaningful connection among poems

 15
Listening and Collaboration

Responds to what others actually say, invites or makes room for other voices, and helps sustain a shared inquiry

 10
Preparation and Engagement

Arrives with annotated texts and usable questions and quotes; remains attentive and involved throughout

 5


A note on participation: The number of times you speak is not a score. To earn a strong grade, you do need to make your thinking audible at some point so that I can assess it. A few substantial contributions can be more valuable than frequent comments that do not move the discussion forward.
